inline.s: Sima Guang of the Song dynasty, when he was five years old, once tried to remove the skin from a walnut. He worked at it for a long time but simply could not get the skin off. Later a maidservant in the household saw this and helped him by soaking the walnut in hot water, so that the skin came off very easily. Just then his elder sister came in from outside and asked him, ‘Did you peel the walnut yourself?’ Sima Guang replied, ‘Yes, I peeled it myself!’ His father heard this and scolded him, ‘A child must not speak falsehoods!’ Sima Guang was startled, and from then on repented and reformed; for the rest of his life he never dared to lie again.

Xu Jiexiaoji of the Song dynasty, when he first paid a visit to Mr. Anding, tilted his head ever so slightly. Mr. Anding said sternly, ‘Your head should be held straight; it must not be crooked.’ Xu immediately repented and understood, saying, ‘If the head must be held straight and not crooked, how then can the mind be allowed to be crooked?’ From that time on, Xu’s mind was never in the least bit slanted. When someone asked him, ‘What is the essential secret of conducting oneself in the world and cultivating oneself?’ he would always write the two large words ‘upright and honest’ for the one who asked.

The great Song dynasty writer Zeng Zigu (Zeng Gong) was on good terms with Wang Anshi. Emperor Shenzong asked Zeng Gong, ‘What do you think of Anshi’s character?’ Zeng Gong replied, ‘Anshi’s writings and conduct are not inferior to those of Yang Xiong of the Han dynasty, but because he is niggardly, he falls short of Yang Xiong.’ The emperor said, ‘Anshi does not set store by wealth and rank; how can you call him niggardly?’ Zeng Gong said, ‘What I call niggardly is that, though Anshi is bold in undertaking affairs and accomplishing things, he is nonetheless stingy about correcting his own faults.’ Hearing this, Emperor Shenzong nodded in agreement with his view.

Alas! Wang Anshi, with the talent of a prime minister, ended by covering up his faults and refusing to acknowledge them, until at last he brought calamity upon the whole realm, harmed the common people, and left behind a name reviled for ten thousand generations. How much more so for those today who are obstinate and self-opinionated and yet without talent, who live amid their faults every day and do not even know to reform!
Though good deeds are plainly before one’s eyes, yet one refuses to go and do them bravely.

The ancients said, ‘By taking what is small one attains the great; by accumulating ones one reaches the myriad.’ Therefore in doing good, what matters most is daily accumulation and steady storing up. When you know a thing is good, do it at once, and do it earnestly and diligently. Laozi said, ‘A nine-story tower begins from a mound of earth piled up bit by bit; a journey of a thousand li begins from a single step.’ If a person can correct one fault each day, he can dissolve one karmic offense; if he can do one good deed each day, he can add one foundation of blessing. The Purple Void Perfected Lord said, ‘The Way is born of stillness, virtue is born of humility, blessing is born of frugality and purity, and life is born of harmony and ease. Calamity comes from many desires, and fault comes from contempt and negligence. Therefore guard the eyes — let them not look at others’ faults; guard the mouth — let it not speak of others’ shortcomings; guard the mind — let it not indulge thoughts of greed and anger; guard the body — let it not follow evil companions. Life is like a candle burning in the wind; at any moment it may be blown out. So always think: after death, where will the spirit go? This body is only a temporary lodging in this dusty world; do not go and create offense upon offense. Know that good and evil both dwell in the mind and never err by a hair’s breadth; and if a person is clever at schemes and contrivances, then Heaven is all the more clever at requital.’ From this we see that if in one day a person hears one word of good, sees one good deed, and does one good act, then that day is not wasted in vain. But if a person plainly sees a good deed before his eyes and will not do it, one knows not what sort of heart, liver, or intestines he has; it is nothing but self-abandonment, self-degradation, wasting one’s life, and cutting oneself off from the world. How foolish indeed!

In the Tang dynasty there was a man named Su Cheng, of a most vicious and intractable nature, who in his whole life never did a single good deed. Whenever he saw in books words of virtue and meritorious conduct, he would surely say, ‘This must be false!’ When he saw others diligently doing good, he would surely laugh and say, ‘This man must be a crafty and wicked villain!’ When Su Cheng reached middle age, his body gradually shrank, until he had to crawl on the ground on his two hands. He ate and slept with the dogs, and so a year passed before he died.

Toward the end of the Zhou dynasty, Duke Huan of Qi once passed by the ruins of the Guo clan and asked an old man living nearby, ‘How did the Guo clan come to decline and perish?’ The old man replied, ‘Because the Guo clan loved what was good and hated what was evil.’ Duke Huan said, ‘To love good and hate evil — how could that lead to decline and ruin?’ The old man said, ‘Because the Guo clan loved good but could not practice it, and hated evil yet could not keep themselves from doing it. For that reason they declined and perished.’

Judging from this story, the people of today have lost their own spirit and cannot awaken to their true nature; moreover, with the myriad conditions crisscrossing and interfering, their minds are weary with running about all day, hard-pressed to cope. One thought comes, another thought goes; in a single day and night there are eight hundred and forty million thoughts. This is like the wind dancing in the sky with nothing to rest upon, or a stone pressing on grass — it stops for a moment, then springs up again. Where is there any day given wholly to doing good? Therefore though one knows that good deeds should be done, one is changed by one’s own desires; even if one preaches the sutras all day long, it is often mixed with fame and gain, like a tree whose leaves flourish on the outside while its roots have already rotted, till at last it destroys and overturns itself. Is this not a great pity?

A fine admonition. The Chan master Tianru Weize of the Yuan dynasty earnestly urged the people of the world, saying: ‘The ancients of virtue often said, “When I see another person die, my heart burns with anxiety as if on fire — not because I am anxious for that other, but because I see that soon it will be my turn.” Such words — who does not know them? But though one knows them, one simply is unwilling to practice. And yet to say you are unwilling to practice is to wrong you; the worthies present here have for the most part begun with earnest effort. It is only that you have not yet reached the point where everything is settled and complete. Where is the fault? The fault lies in not being fierce enough, not being diligent enough, not being firm enough, not being enduring enough. You merely rouse a resolve for a while, and soon after you retreat. Hence it is said, “The Buddha-dharma is not much; it is the long-lasting person that is hard to find.” If practitioners of the Way were as earnest as on the day they first resolved, even becoming a Buddha would be more than enough. Therefore it is said that he who is unchanging from beginning to end is truly a great man. How many people today can be unchanging from beginning to end? Often ten people yield five already fallen away from their resolve for the Way! If we examine the causes of their falling away, each has his own encumbrances. What then are the encumbrances? There are three. First, whether monk or lay, man or woman, everyone is encumbered by body and mouth. Next, those with family are encumbered by their families, and those with a livelihood are encumbered by their livelihood. These three encumbrances — they are what kill the people of the world! All the people of the world suffer these three encumbrances, and so they are busy for a lifetime, bustling for a lifetime, toiling for a lifetime, slaving for a lifetime, and passing by a lifetime in emptiness. Moreover, because of these three encumbrances they give rise to measureless greed, anger, and delusion, and thereby create measureless great and small evil deeds. Through such karmic retribution they fall into the bitter sea of the three realms and the eight difficulties, transmigrating in birth and death, suffering measureless misery, unable to attain deliverance. Though they suffer measureless misery, they never awaken; and those who do not awaken are so because they are not enlightened. What is it they are not enlightened about? They are not enlightened that body, family, and livelihood are not their own. Now as to your body not being yours, you do not yet believe it. Let this mountain monk now, with all candor, spell it out for you from the beginning. When you first entered your mother’s womb and took on this life, you were but a single consciousness-spirit; where was there ever a body? This body is nothing but a lump of dull flesh formed by the union of father’s essence and mother’s blood, originally without perception; it knew neither pain nor itch, neither cold nor heat, neither hunger nor fullness, neither bitterness nor joy. When this consciousness-spirit attached itself to that lump of dull flesh, from then on it knew pain and itch, cold and heat, hunger and fullness, bitterness and joy; and after it left the mother’s womb it simply took this as its own and called it “my body.” The principle and the fact I have just set forth — that this body is not my own — you thereupon absolutely refuse to believe. Therefore the Buddhas and patriarchs, in compassion for the foolishness of living beings, again earnestly and kindly say to you: “This is not your body! It is a stinking skin-bag formed of essence and blood. It is not under your control, not at your command; even birth, aging, sickness, and death are not arranged by you. How do we know this is so? Just as after you first entered the womb and dwelt in your mother’s belly, you changed every seven days, developing in due order into the five organs and six viscera, the hundred limbs and nine orifices, the four limbs and six sense-roots, sinews, bones, skin, and flesh, gradually taking shape; and even your coming forth from the womb was borne along by the warm wind and driven by karmic power — while you knew nothing of it, and it was never commanded or arranged by you. After birth, when you grow to thirty or forty, your hair turns white, your teeth loosen, your face turns sallow, your flesh becomes thin; all these come gradually, and the signs of old age then appear. Next sickness arrives; and since sickness has come, death follows in its train. So change upon change and ruin upon ruin — each and all are beyond your control. You too were unwilling that it should be so, but you simply cannot manage it. Consider that from birth to death you have spent upon this stinking skin-bag no small measure of love and affection, tending it in every way, cherishing and pitying it in every way, treating and settling it in every way; yet it is ungrateful and repays you with such loathsomeness. And there is that which is even more repulsive: for example, on a hot summer day a strong and hale fellow suddenly takes an acute illness at dusk and dies; by the second or third watch of the night his corpse reeks and overpowers those nearby, so that none can approach. In haste they place the body in a coffin, close it up, and before the bell of dawn they hurriedly carry it out and burn it. Even his dearest and most beloved family do not allow him to linger a moment longer.” Judging by this, last night he was still a hale man, and this morning he is a heap of bone-ash; and no one knows where his consciousness-spirit has gone. So sudden is the change, and it is not in your power. Since it is your body, it ought to be governed by you; since it is not governed by you, how can you falsely take it to be your body? This is only to be burdened by it for nothing and to retreat from your resolve for the Way. Your family is likewise: each drags along a stinking skin-bag, each is unfree, each is beyond the other’s control; and once impermanence arrives, none can take the place of another. While alive, they are bound together by affection and are called “family”; but once their eyes are closed, they do not recognize one another. How can you falsely take them as your family, be burdened by them, and retreat from your resolve? Your livelihood is likewise: while your eyes are open and your legs are strong, you scheme and manage, hoard and guard your property, thinking that for a hundred thousand years you will enjoy its use. Who would know that when one breath fails, not a hair’s worth can be carried along! How can you falsely take it as your livelihood, be burdened by it, and retreat from your resolve? Since you have now heard these truths, you should turn back the light and break through, awaken to yourself with sorrow. With regard to these three encumbrances, do not grasp them, do not cling to them, do not covet them. Dwell in your allotted portion, be content with your lot, and pass the days as they come. You must turn your thoughts and, with regard to the great matter of birth and death, rouse yourself to fierce and vigorous diligence. And let your resolve for the Way be firm and enduring, and in this matter strive to fathom it thoroughly.’
Having committed a crime oneself, one refuses to acknowledge it; instead one drags in others, hoping to cast off the responsibility for one’s own offense.

The crime was committed by oneself; but when the affair comes to light, one drags in others to bear the blame and shifts it upon them. This is what the proverb calls “pulling a man down into the water.” The motive is either to cover up one’s own wrongdoings, or to take revenge by framing one’s enemy. One does not realize that one’s own fault can never be concealed, and that to falsely accuse another can never succeed. It only adds to one’s own sin. Even if by luck one escapes the punishment of the law, one cannot escape the judgment of Heaven.

Zhao Ye once stood by and watched Jia Yi slaughter an ox. After Jia Yi died, he said to the judge of the underworld, ‘When I slaughtered the ox, Zhao Ye was also beside me helping me kill it.’ He said this hoping that Zhao Ye would share the burden of his guilt. When Zhao Ye’s soul was seized by the ghostly soldiers and brought to the underworld, he could scarcely recognize Jia Yi. Soon he saw a great mirror, about a zhang across, hanging in the air; and in it was clearly visible Jia Yi holding a knife and slaughtering the ox, while Zhao Ye leaned by the door with a look of pity and reluctance in his heart. Only then was Jia Yi willing to admit his guilt, and Zhao Ye’s soul was able to return to the world of the living.

According to the Buddha’s words: ‘All living beings in the world are subject to birth and death in succession. At the moment of death, before the warmth of the body has departed, all the good and evil done in one’s lifetime suddenly appear before one. As a rule, the states that appear at death are precisely the states of one’s ordinary mind.’ Therefore the jewel of guilt held by Bodhisattva Ksitigarbha is my own jewel of the mind, and the mirror of karma before King Yama is my own mirror of the mind. Moreover, when we do an unwholesome deed, an impression is left in our minds, lingering and haunting us and never wearing away. How then can one recklessly drag others in and falsely accuse them?

To deliberately obstruct such arts as medicine, divination, astrology, physiognomy, or any single skill or profession, so that those who practice them cannot use their learning to support their families and help the world.

Medicine, divination, astrology, and physiognomy, as well as any single skill or craft, may all be counted as practical arts. Those of shallow skill may use these arts to support their families; those of deep skill may use them to save and help others. If one deliberately obstructs and blocks such arts so that they cannot be practiced, this shows one’s mind is not broad and generous, and it will result in many in the land being cold, hungry, and out of work. As for heterodox teachers and unskilled physicians who harm right teaching and ruin lives, and such practices as refining elixirs and calcining mercury, these cannot be excused by this principle and should instead be forbidden. The households of scholars must strictly guard their doors; all such women as the three nuns and six matchmakers should be refused all contact; and even if there must be contact, one should pay attention to the uprightness of their character. This too is a method of straightening the root and guarding against trouble at its very outset.

While Zhai Qianyou was alive, he was quite renowned for his ability to summon spirits. Whenever he thought of the commandery of Yun’an, there were as many as fifteen places where the river currents were dangerous. So he summoned the spirits of the rapids, planning to level these perilous shoals so that they would no longer be dangerous. Fourteen of the rapids’ spirits answered his summons. Alone there was a female spirit of the rapids, wearing a tall hat and a long robe, who boldly admonished Zhai Qianyou, saying: ‘From what I observe, your intention in leveling the shoals is merely to make it convenient for the boats coming and going. But you do not know that those who ply the boat trade reap extremely rich profits; even if they spend a bit more, it is no loss to them. Yet there are three or four hundred poor households living along the river. They have no fields to till and no mulberry trees on which to raise silkworms; all of them depend on the labor of towing boats through the dangerous shoals to make a living. If today these shoals are leveled, it will indeed be more convenient for the boatmen; but for those poor people who live by the river and depend on towing boats for their livelihood, on what will they rely to get by in the future? The intention of the Most High is surely not like this. I fear that you, Sir, will in the end incur blame because of this; I cannot but worry for you, and so I make this suggestion, hoping that you will change your decision.’ The celestial master Zhai sighed and said, ‘Your consideration is so thorough and far-sighted that I am not able to equal you.’ Thereupon he again commanded the fourteen spirits of the rapids each to restore the shoals to their former danger.

From this story we can see that not only must the practical arts not be obstructed and blocked, but even the small trades by which people earn their food through their own labor should be allowed to circulate and flow; one should leave them some room in every case, so that their lives are not trapped by cold and hunger. This is how a benevolent person uses his heart.
Toward the sages and worthies of antiquity one does not offer respectful veneration, but instead dares to slander them at will.

There are two kinds of people who delight in mocking and slandering the sages and worthies. One kind, through their own folly, does not know the great and far-reaching influence of the sages’ teaching upon the world. Such people are like one hiding in a jar and looking at the sky through the jar’s mouth, yet complaining that the sky is so small. The other kind are those of worldly cleverness and eloquent wit, who rely on their intelligence and persuasive speech to incite and mislead others into slandering the sages; these are like grasping for the moon in the water, laboring in vain. And the sages are not in the least affected by their incitement and slander. The sages and worthies referred to here are the sages of the three teachings: Confucianism, Buddhism, and Taoism. Confucianism teaches by means of uprightness, Buddhism teaches by means of greatness, and Taoism teaches by means of reverence. We see that all three teachings are skilled at protecting living beings and abhor killing them. All are manifestations of a benevolent heart; all require that one treat others as one treats oneself; all are equal, impartial, and selfless, curbing anger and moderating desire, forbidding faults and preventing error; all require the inner cultivation and discipline of the self; and all can, like thunder, shake living beings from their confusion and awaken their wisdom. Likewise all can serve the function of transforming customs and enlightening the people. In a word, the principle of the world consists of but two paths, good and evil; and the original intent of the three teachings is nothing other than to teach people to correct their faults and follow the good. If we speak of the inner cultivation of the mind, then the three teachings all return to the One. Therefore Emperor Xiaozong of the Song, in reply to Han Yu’s essay that rejected Buddhism and Taoism, said: ‘Govern the mind with Buddhism, govern the body with Taoism, and govern the world with Confucianism.’ Emperor Xiaozong truly understood that mind, body, and world are alike of equal importance, and that not one of them may be left ungoverned. If this is so, then how could the three teachings tolerate one of them being absent? They should all exist together at the same time!

The Confucians of today either cite the sages to refute and deny Buddhism, or consider Buddhism as excelling the sages. The monks and Taoists of today either destroy Taoism for the sake of Buddhism, or criticize Buddhism for the sake of Taoism. In short, they are all led astray by the attachment of their own views and are wrongly discriminating the great Way. How could they understand that the three teachings are in the end not at all different? What is most to be feared is that people form mistaken ideas and, by their own intention, make conjectures and dispute with an agitated mind. Whereas a person of truly great wisdom, able to calm his mind and thoroughly fuse these principles, tracing them to their root and straight to their source, will know that Buddhism’s teaching to illuminate the mind and see one’s own nature, to cast off delusion and seek awakening; Taoism’s teaching to purify the mind and reduce desires, to accumulate merit and practice virtue; and Confucianism’s teaching to rectify the mind and make the will sincere — all are able to gather, receive, and transform living beings without conflict. In a word, they all but lead people to the Way. What further names and forms are there to cling to? Hence we know that the three teachings are all the right teaching, and for a million years together the eyes of all sentient and intelligent beings, and the standard of truth. Why be so foolish as to slander the sages and worthies, creating the evil cause for falling into the hell of the pulled-out tongue in the next life? As for the scriptures, books, and written papers, these are where the spirit of the sages and worthies is entrusted; and those who trample upon scriptures, books, and written papers bear the same guilt as those who revile the sages.

Gao Zhishou did not believe in the immortals or the Buddha, and exerted every effort to vilify them. He once pasted his wall with the Lotus Sutra. When someone presented him with a Buddha image, Gao Zhishou said: ‘This Buddha image can be made into utensils for use!’ So he sawed it up and made it into ten ring-shaped ornaments. Later, because he ridiculed and criticized the policies of the imperial court, the emperor issued a decree sending him to the Ministry of Justice for trial and sentencing. He was finally sentenced to be cut in two at the waist, and the sentence was carried out in the marketplace.

The great Ming-dynasty general Qi Jiguang recited the Diamond Sutra in his daily practice. One day he suddenly dreamed of a dead soldier who begged him to recite one roll of the Diamond Sutra to increase his merit in the netherworld. When Qi Jiguang arose in the morning, he recited a full roll of the Diamond Sutra for the deceased soldier. Yet again he dreamed of the soldier, who said to him: ‘I am indebted to you for your great kindness, General, in reciting a roll of the Diamond Sutra for me. But I obtained only half a roll’s merit, because there were mixed in the two words “not needed”!’ Qi Jiguang thought for a long time before he understood where the two words ‘not needed’ came from. It turned out that while he was reciting, his maidservant brought him tea and cakes; he waved his hand to decline, and though he did not speak it aloud, in his mind there were the words ‘not needed.’ So the next morning he shut his door and recited the sutra. Later he again dreamed of the deceased soldier, who thanked him, saying: ‘Reporting to you, General, I have now attained deliverance!’
From this story we can understand that in reciting the scriptures of the sages one may not even mix in a single wandering thought; much less may one slander the sages.
When one meets a man of the Way and of virtue, one does not respect him or draw near him, but instead violates and bullies him.

People of virtue in the world — such as Confucian scholars who read books and understand principle, or monks and Taoists who practice austerities assiduously — their words can serve as a model for the world, and their conduct can serve as an example for the world. These virtuous people stand out above the crowd because they are the very condensation of the upright energy of heaven and earth. If we love and respect them, it is already not enough; how can we violate and bully them?

The Chan master Guoqing expounded the sutras and preached the Dharma to deliver sentient beings. But a certain official, who had never believed in Buddhism, bound the master and struck him twenty strokes with a plank. That night the official dreamed that his dead father was very angry, and weeping, said to him: ‘How dare you insult a Chan master! Because of this, King Yama has also struck me twenty lashes of an iron whip, and even your official rank has been stripped away.’

When Chunyu Chongde was twenty years old, he entered the school palace to study. His nature was exceedingly strange and perverse, and whenever there was a virtuous scholar he would surely subject him to great bullying and denigration. One night he suddenly saw a deity, who said to him: ‘You have made every kind of effort to violate and bully virtuous men, so I have come to take away your intelligence!’ When the deity finished, he drew his knife and struck; and Chunyu Chongde fell senseless to the ground. After he woke, he was as dull as an idiot, and within a few years he died.

When Zhang Liang of the Han dynasty was young, he once traveled to Xiapi to amuse himself. There was an old man on a bridge whose shoe fell down to the foot of the bridge. The old man said to Zhang Liang: ‘Young man, go under the bridge and pick up my shoe for me.’ Zhang Liang, considering the old man’s age, reluctantly repressed his temper and went down beneath the bridge to pick up the shoe. After he had picked it up, the old man raised his foot and said: ‘Young man, put it on for me.’ Zhang Liang knelt and put the shoe on for the old man. The old man said: ‘You are a lad who can be taught!’ Then he brought out a scroll and said to Zhang Liang: ‘If you read this scroll, you can become a teacher of emperors.’ Having said this, the old man left without ever turning his head. Zhang Liang looked at the scroll; it was the military classic of the Grand Duke Jiang. Thereupon he studied it earnestly, and later helped Emperor Gaozu of Han, Liu Bang, win the empire, and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Liu.

From this story we can learn that people of virtue can bring about the success of many talented persons; those who violate and insult men of virtue are like one throwing dust against the wind, or stretching out a hand to block the sky — they only let others see how utterly they overestimate themselves.
To shoot and kill flying birds, and to hunt and capture running beasts.

‘To shoot’ does not refer only to shooting with bow and arrow. All that is done with firelocks, bird-guns, poisoned crossbows, pellet bows, sticky poles, snares, and nets also counts as shooting. Whether to make money or to satisfy the appetites of mouth and belly, one sets traps of killing all around, so that the flying birds lose their lives — some with heads cut off, some with breasts run through. How great is their suffering! We ought to double our loving-kindness in delivering and protecting them. Those who eat their flesh — how can they bear to forge this enmity that is certain to be repaid hereafter, and to use them as dishes that could be reduced or dispensed with? And those who make a living by trapping and killing birds and beasts — why would they take the trouble to create this endless enmity in order to earn these limited profits?

A certain Mr. Dong delighted in catching flying birds with nets, and after catching them, ran a bamboo stick through the birds’ heads, burned their feathers with straw, and sold them for money. The number of birds he killed was beyond counting. When Dong grew old, he fell ill with a strange disease. His whole body broke out in a thick skin, coarse and wrinkled like tree bark. When it itched, he used straw to burn the thick skin to stop the itch; when his head ached, he had people beat it with a bamboo stick. In the end he died from this strange illness. And Liu Dong’er made a speciality of shooting flying birds with a crossbow; there was no counting the birds he shot down. One day, leaning by the door to shoot sparrows, he happened to feel an itch in his ear and used an arrowhead to scratch it. Then suddenly a gust of wind slammed the door, which struck the hand that held the arrow; the arrowhead pierced through his ear and the blood gushed out like a stream. And so Liu Dong’er died.
Alas! Shooting oneself with the arrow, burning oneself with the straw — each and every one is the evil karma that one has oneself created. How wondrously exact is the retribution!

In the Tang dynasty, Wei Gao kept a parrot. Whenever this parrot heard the recitation of the Buddha’s name, it would become extremely excited and listen intently; and when told to recite, it would loudly chant Namo Amitabha Buddha. One day the parrot stood upright and passed away. After cremation there were found ten relics, and Wei Gao erected a stupa to bury it. Again, during the Yuanyou era of the Song dynasty, there was a monk who kept a mynah bird that always recited the Buddha’s name along with the monk. One day the mynah lowered its head, folded its wings, and stood up and passed away. The abbot of the temple, taking pity on it, buried it. Suddenly there grew from the place where it was buried a blue lotus flower, of extraordinary fragrance. Everyone, greatly astonished, dug open the mound where the mynah was buried, and found the lotus had actually grown from the mynah’s tongue-root! All the people of the prefecture came to see it, and the prefect composed a special verse in its honor: ‘Heaven produced this wonder-bird, eight-eight its name; it learned the monk’s mouth, chanting Amitabha the same. If this feathered creature could the unborn patience gain, how can we who are human fall short and feel no shame?’

Observing these two stories, the creatures of the world, great and small, are all sentient beings; and our Buddha, in his great compassion, receives and cherishes them all impartially. Why then should people still slaughter the lives of creatures?

Mr. Yan Maoyou of the Ming dynasty said: ‘The people of today all say that Heaven produced the myriad things to nourish mankind, and so these flying birds and running beasts were meant from the very beginning to be eaten by people. They do not know that man too is one of the creatures growing between heaven and earth. If a person can cultivate his true nature and kindly protect living beings, then he is worthy to be called “the most spiritual of all creatures”; otherwise, what difference is there between him and the beasts? Moreover, if a person does not practice according to the right teaching, he cannot escape the six realms but still transmigrates within them. The animal of this life may have been a human being in a former life, and the person who gains a human body in this life may have been an animal in a former life. Thus greed, anger, and slaughter, devouring one another along the road of birth and death, are things to be most feared; and once one enters the netherworld, how does one know that the one who today hunts and captures the running beast will not in turn be pursued by the beasts he has slain?’

Someone may ask: ‘If people did not kill living beings or eat meat, would not the birds and beasts then fill the world? For example, wolves, jackals, tigers, and leopards would eat people — would this not be raising beasts to harm mankind?’ I answer him: ‘The Buddha said: if a person possesses loving-kindness and merit, then all weapons, fire, water, and soldiers cannot harm him, and all fierce beasts and venomous insects cannot harm him. In former times there was an evil king who drove a herd of fierce elephants toward the Buddha, seeking to kill him; but the Buddha’s mind gave rise to loving-kindness, pitying the evil king and the elephants for their ignorance. At that moment the herd of elephants saw the Buddha’s five fingers transform into a lion’s roar, and the elephants all fell prostrate before the Buddha. This is why the Nirvana Sutra so greatly praises the merit of loving-kindness; for when loving-kindness reaches its utmost, it can transform even the most savage beasts of the world!’

In the time of Emperor Guangwu of the Eastern Han, within the jurisdiction of Hongnong commandery there were many tigers. The governor ordered the people to set many traps and take up bows and arrows to guard against the harm the tigers caused; yet the harm wrought by the tigers became even worse. When Liu Kun became the governor of Hongnong commandery, he said: ‘The menace of the tigers has been brought about by tyrannical government.’ Thereupon he ordered the people to fill in all the traps and snap their bows and arrows, and actively to practice benevolent governance and to feel for the hardships of the common people. The tigers thereupon crossed the river in droves and left the commandery of Hongnong.
